newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-Fairfax slams govt media plans.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Fairfax slams govt media plans.

text.p: John Fairfax Holdings Ltd chairman Sir Laurence Street said on Thursday that any government proposal leading to the break-up of the Fairfax newspaper group would be against Australia's national interest.
Quoting Canberra sources, various newspapers said planned changes to media ownership laws could lead to Fairfax being taken over by Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer.

"To create a climate where Fairfax is dismembered by being weakened in the way of this apparent divestiture, seems to me to be utterly inimical to the national interest," said Street, who has been Fairfax chairman since 1994.

Fairfax is Australia's oldest newspaper group and is the country's second largest newspaper publisher behind News Ltd, the local offshoot of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd, which has about 66 percent of the domestic newspaper market.
"It is the only creditable competition to News Ltd, competition is the very lifeblood of our democracy and our commercial activities," Street said in a telephone interview.

Street said he has not spoken to the government about its media rule proposals. Both Packer and News Ltd have discussed media rule changes recently with the government.

"The major financial journal in this country being put in play to a English company that wants to use it as a spearhead into Asia, well it literally leaves me appalled as an Australian that this can be contemplated," Street said.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday confirmed the government was looking at allowing television proprietors to own one newspaper each in major capital city markets.
"A whole lot of things including that is being looked at, a whole lot of things," Howard told radio 2UE.
Fairfax has long been seen as a takeover target by Packer and until last year, Murdoch, who once referred to its classified advertising revenue as "rivers of gold."
Street said he did not see a need for any further media ownership concentration in Australia.
"We don't represent a major monopoly, we don't own television stations, we are a dynamic and growing newspaper company," said Street.

Fairfax largest shareholder is New Zealand investment group Brierley Investments Ltd, which holds about 20 percent of Fairfax. Brierley bought the stake from Canadian and U.K. media baron Conrad Black.
The Liberal-National government abandoned a pre-election promise of a public review of the media ownership, opting for a closed review when it won office in March 1996.

"It is a pity that we didn't have the public inquiry which was contemplated before the last election," said Street, who has been on the Fairfax board since it was bought out of receivership in 1991 by a consortium led by Black, the owner of

Currently, television owners are banned from owning more than 15 percent of a newspaper in the same major market and vice versa. Foreigners are limited to 15 percent of television stations and 25 percent of newspapers.
The reports on Thursday said the government planned to raise foreign limits, possibly to 35 percent industry-wide.
These changes would probably mean that Packer would have to sell the Australian Financial Review newspaper.

Executives from Pearson Plc, publishers of the Financial Times, and The Economist magazine have held talks with the government in recent weeks and are believed to be keen potential buyers of Australia's business daily.

Fairfax publishes The Sydney Morning Herald and Melbourne Age daily broadsheet newspapers along with the Australian Financial Review business daily. It also publishes magazines and regional newspapers.
The newspaper reports said the Liberal-National government was planning to ease media cross-ownership and foreign ownership laws, which would allow Murdoch and Packer to expand their media empires.
Packer has a controlling interest in Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, which is also Australia's largest magazine publisher.
